introduction-geography-for-strategy.core: Strategy without a shared picture becomes an opinion contest. Maps (Wardley) and grids (SWOT) give teams a common view of the landscape, so decisions are argued from evidence.

first_principles.problem: "Serverless!" "No, Kubernetes!" Neither side can point to a shared frame showing why one fits better.
truths: Positions without context can't be compared.
derivation: **Draw** the landscape everyone is talking about.
Use it to **locate** options and **anticipate** movement.
Argue about the map, not about preferences.

analogy.title: Generals with a map
analogy.story: Armies plan with a terrain map in front of everyone, not by shouting directions.
analogy.breaks: Terrain is physical and static. Tech landscapes evolve constantly.

example.title: Serverless vs Kubernetes debate
example.scenario: A team argues for an hour.

steps.label: Outcome
steps.detail: Debate shifts to where value lies, not tool preference.

example.outcome: decisions are grounded in a shared view.

check.a: It gives everyone the same frame, so options are compared on evidence rather than preference.

the-problem-strategic-visualization-solv.core: Without a shared picture, build-vs-buy debates go in circles because each person reasons from a different, unstated view of the landscape. Visualisation makes those assumptions explicit.

first_principles.problem: Engineer A: "Build our own pipeline, ArgoCD doesn't fit." Engineer B: "Building is a waste." They aren't disagreeing about facts; they're assuming different things about maturity and value.
truths: Making them visible lets them be challenged.
derivation: Surface each person's **assumptions** (what users need, how mature each component is).
Put them on **one picture**.
Resolve disagreement on the **specific point** where views differ.

analogy.title: Two people describing an elephant
analogy.story: One touches the trunk, one the leg; both are right and both are wrong. A picture of the whole elephant ends the argument.
analogy.breaks: Elephants are concrete. Strategic maps are models, so they're only as good as the input.

example.title: Custom pipeline vs ArgoCD

steps.label: Pinpoint
steps.detail: The only real disagreement was one workflow step.

example.outcome: the team builds only the small unique part.

check.q: What do circular build-vs-buy debates usually lack?
check.a: A shared, explicit view of user needs and component maturity.

wardley-mapping-the-two-axes.core: A Wardley map plots components by visibility to the user (vertical value chain) and by evolution (horizontal: genesis → custom → product → commodity). Position tells you whether to build, buy or outsource.

first_principles.problem: Teams build commodity things (logging, auth) in-house and buy things that should differentiate them, because they lack a way to see maturity.
truths: Users see some components directly, others not at all.
Commodity should be bought; novelty may be built.
derivation: **Y-axis**: start with the user need at top, chain down to dependencies.
**X-axis**: Genesis (novel), Custom-built, Product, Commodity/utility.
**Build** genesis/custom where it differentiates; **buy/rent** product and commodity.

analogy.title: A topographic map
analogy.story: Instead of height and position, you plot how visible something is to customers and how mature it is.
analogy.breaks: Mountains don't move. Components drift rightward over time.

steps.label: Strategy
steps.detail: Invest in recommendations; buy payments; rent compute.

check.q: What are the four evolution stages?
check.a: Genesis, custom-built, product (and rental), and commodity (utility).

reading-a-wardley-map-movement-and-gamep.core: Maps matter for movement: components evolve rightward, commoditisation enables new higher-order systems, and inertia resists change. Read where things will be in 2–3 years and act ahead of it.

first_principles.problem: Teams keep investing in custom solutions for things about to become commodities, and are surprised when a managed service wipes out their advantage.
truths: Commodity components enable new innovation above them.
Organisations resist moving off what they built.
derivation: Ask **where each component will be in 2–3 years**.
Plan to **migrate** custom work as it commoditises.
Use **gameplay**: open-source to commoditise a rival's advantage, build on new utilities.
Watch your own **inertia**.

analogy.title: Electricity becoming a utility
analogy.story: Factories once ran their own generators. When grid power became a utility, those who switched early could focus on what they made.
analogy.breaks: Electricity commoditised over decades; tech can commoditise in a couple of years.

example.title: Self-hosted Kubernetes in 2026
example.scenario: A team runs its own control planes.

steps.label: Move
steps.detail: Shift effort to developer platform features above Kubernetes.

example.outcome: effort moves to where differentiation now lies.

check.q: Why does inertia matter on a Wardley map?
check.a: Organisations resist moving off past investments even when components have commoditised.

swot-analysis-for-technology-decisions.core: SWOT sorts factors into internal Strengths and Weaknesses and external Opportunities and Threats. Applied with engineering specifics, it structures technology decisions quickly.

first_principles.problem: SWOTs often fill with vague platitudes ('great team', 'competition') that don't inform the decision.
truths: Internal factors are controllable; external aren't.
derivation: **Strengths**: e.g. team has deep Postgres expertise.
**Weaknesses**: e.g. no on-call experience with Kafka.
**Opportunities**: e.g. managed service now available in our region.
**Threats**: e.g. vendor price increases, compliance changes.
Keep each item **specific and evidence-based**.

analogy.title: A pre-match analysis
analogy.story: A coach lists the team's strengths and weaknesses and the opponent's and the weather's likely effects before choosing tactics.
analogy.breaks: Sports matches are short. Tech SWOTs should be revisited as conditions change.

example.title: Adopting Kafka

steps.label: Insight
steps.detail: The weakness is covered by the opportunity.

example.outcome: a quick, structured decision with specific inputs.

check.q: What's the difference between weaknesses and threats?
check.a: Weaknesses are internal to your team or system; threats come from outside.

combining-wardley-maps-and-swot.core: Wardley maps show the landscape and where it's moving; SWOT shows your capabilities and risks within it. Draw the map first, then run SWOT on the key components to choose a move.

first_principles.problem: Using one framework alone gives half the picture: maps without capability analysis, or SWOTs without landscape context.
truths: Landscape and capability are different questions.
derivation: **1.** Draw the Wardley map; mark components that are moving.
**2.** Run SWOT on the components at stake.
**3.** Choose moves that use strengths and opportunities and cover weaknesses and threats.
**4.** Record and revisit.

analogy.title: Map and compass
analogy.story: The map shows the terrain; the compass and your fitness tell you which route you can actually take.
analogy.breaks: Hikers know their fitness. Teams must honestly assess their capabilities.

example.title: Observability strategy
example.outcome: a decision justified by both landscape and capability.

check.q: Which question does each framework answer?
check.a: Wardley: what's the landscape and where is it moving? SWOT: what are our capabilities and risks within it?
